{{Short description|Theorem of dominion in abstract algebra}}

'''Isbell's zigzag theorem''', a theorem of [[abstract algebra]] characterizing the notion of a dominion, was introduced by American [[mathematician]] [[John R. Isbell]] in 1966.<ref>{{harv|Isbell|1966}}</ref> [[#Dominion|Dominion]] is a concept in [[Semigroup|semigroup theory]], within the study of the properties of [[epimorphism]]s. For example, let {{mvar|U}} be a subsemigroup of {{mvar|S}} containing {{mvar|U}}, the [[inclusion map]] <math>U \hookrightarrow S</math> is an epimorphism [[if and only if]] <math>\rm{Dom}_S (U) = S</math>, furthermore, a map <math>\alpha \colon S \to T</math> is an [[epimorphism]] if and only if <math>\rm{Dom}_T (\rm{im} \; \alpha) = T</math>.{{R|Howie1996}} The categories of rings and semigroups are [[#Application|examples of categories with non-surjective epimorphism]], and the Zig-zag theorem gives necessary and sufficient conditions for determining whether or not a given morphism is epi.{{R|Higgins1988}} Proofs of this theorem are [[topological]] in nature, beginning with {{harvtxt|Isbell|1966}} for [[semigroups]], and continuing by {{harvtxt|Philip|1974}}, completing Isbell's original proof.{{R|Higgins1988}}{{R|Higgins1990}}{{R|Hoffman}} The pure algebraic proofs were given by {{harvtxt|Howie|1976}} and {{harvtxt|Storrer|1976}}.{{R|Higgins1988}}{{R|Higgins1990}}{{refn|group=note|These pure algebraic proofs were based on the tensor product characterization of the dominant elements for monoid by {{harvtxt|Stenström|1971}}.<ref name=Storrer1976>{{harv|Storrer|1976}}</ref>{{R|Higgins1990}}}}

== Statement ==
=== Zig-zag ===
[[File:Zigzag theorem 2.svg|thumb|upright|The dashed line is the spine of the zig-zag.]]
Zig-zag:{{R|HowieIsbell1967}}<ref name=Howie1996>{{harv|Howie|1996}}</ref><ref>{{harv|Hall|1982}}</ref><ref name=Higgins1986>{{harv|Higgins|1986}}</ref>{{R|Higgins2016}}{{refn|group=note|See Hoffman<ref name=Hoffman>{{harv|Hoffman|2008}}</ref> or Mitchell<ref>{{harv|Mitchell|1972}}</ref> for [[commutative diagram]].}} If {{mvar|U}} is a submonoid of a [[monoid]] (or a subsemigroup of a semigroup) {{mvar|S}}, then a system of equalities;

<math>\begin{align}

d &= x_1 u_1, &u_1 &= v_1 y_1 \\

x_{i - 1} v_{i - 1} &= x_i u_i, &u_i y_{i - 1} &= v_i y_i \; (i = 2, \dots, m) \\

x_{m} v_{m} &= u_{m+1}, &u_{m + 1} y_{m} &= d

\end{align}</math>

in which <math>u_1, \dots , u_{m + 1}, v_1, \dots , v_{m} \in U</math> and <math>x_1, \dots , x_{m}, y_1, \dots , y_{m} \in S</math>, is called a zig-zag of length {{mvar|m}} in {{mvar|S}} over {{mvar|U}} with value {{mvar|d}}. By the spine of the zig-zag we mean the ordered {{mvar|(2m + 1)}}-[[tuple]] <math>(u_1,v_1,u_2,v_2,\dots,u_{m},v_{m}, u_{m+1})</math>.

=== Dominion ===
Dominion:{{R|Hoffman}}{{R|Storrer1976}} Let {{mvar|U}} be a submonoid of a monoid (or a subsemigroup of a semigroup) {{mvar|S}}. The dominion <math>\rm{Dom}_S (U)</math> is the set of all elements <math>s \in S</math> such that, for all homomorphisms <math>f, g : S \to T</math> coinciding on {{mvar|U}}, <math>f(s) = g(s)</math>.

We call a subsemigroup {{mvar|U}} of a semigroup {{mvar|S}} closed 
if <math>\rm{Dom}_S (U) = U</math>, and dense if <math>\rm{Dom}_S (U) = S</math>.{{R|Howie1996}}<ref>{{harv|Higgins|1983}}</ref>

=== Isbell's zigzag theorem ===
Isbell's zigzag theorem:<ref>{{harv|Howie|1996|loc=Theorem 1.2.}}</ref>

If {{mvar|U}} is a submonoid of a monoid {{mvar|S}} then <math>d \in \rm{Dom}_S (U)</math> if and only if either <math>d \in U</math> or there exists a zig-zag in {{mvar|S}} over {{mvar|U}} with value {{mvar|d}} that is, there is a sequence of factorizations of {{mvar|d}} of the form

<math>d = x_1 u_1=x_1 v_1 y_1 = x_2 u_2 y_1 = x_2 v_2 y_2 = \cdots = x_{m} v_{m} y_{m} = u_{m+1} y_{m}</math>

This statement also holds for [[semigroups]].{{R|HowieIsbell1967}}<ref>{{harv|Higgins|1985}}</ref>{{R|Higgins1986}}<ref name=Higgins1990>{{harv|Higgins|1990}}</ref>{{R|Higgins2016}}

For monoids, this theorem can be written more concisely:<ref>{{harv|Stenström|1971}}</ref>{{R|Howie1996}}<ref>{{harv|Renshaw|2002}}</ref>

Let {{mvar|S}} be a monoid, let {{mvar|U}} be a submonoid of {{mvar|S}}, and let <math>d \in S</math>. Then <math>d \in \mathrm{Dom}_{S} (U)</math> if and only if  <math>d \otimes 1 = 1 \otimes d</math> in the [[tensor product]] <math>S \otimes_{U} S</math>.

== Application ==
*Let {{mvar|U}} be a commutative subsemigroup of a semigroup {{mvar|S}}. Then <math>\rm{Dom}_S (U)</math> is commutative.<ref name = Higgins2016>{{harv|Higgins|2016}}</ref>
*Every epimorphism <math>\alpha \colon S \to T</math> from a finite commutative semigroup {{mvar|S}} to another semigroup {{mvar|T}} is surjective.{{R|Higgins2016}}
*[[Inverse semigroup]]s are absolutely closed.<ref name =HowieIsbell1967>{{harv|Howie|Isbell|1967|loc=Theorem 2.3.}}</ref>
*Example of non-surjective epimorphism in the [[category of rings]]:<ref name = Higgins1988>{{harv|Higgins|1988}}</ref>  The inclusion <math>i: (\mathbb{Z},\cdot)\hookrightarrow (\mathbb{Q},\cdot)</math> is an epimorphism in the category of all rings and ring homomorphisms by proving that any pair of [[ring homomorphism]]s <math>\beta, \gamma: \mathbb{Q} \to R</math> to any ring <math>R</math> which agree on <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> are fact equal.
{{collapse top|A proof sketch for example of non-surjective epimorphism in the category of rings by using zig-zag}}

We show that: Let <math>\beta, \gamma</math> to be ring homomorphisms, and <math>n,m \in \mathbb{Z}</math>, <math>n \neq 0</math>. When <math>\beta(m) = \gamma(m)</math> for all <math>m \in \mathbb{Z}</math>, then <math>\beta\left(\frac{m}{n}\right) = \gamma\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)</math> for all <math>\frac{m}{n} \in \mathbb{Q}</math>.

<math>
\begin{align}
\beta\left(\frac{m}{n}\right) 
&=\beta\left(\frac{1}{n} \cdot m \right) 
= \beta\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\cdot \beta(m)\\
&= \beta\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\cdot \gamma(m)
= \beta\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\cdot \gamma \left(mn \cdot \frac{1}{n} \right)\\
&= \beta\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\cdot \gamma(mn) \cdot \gamma\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)
= \beta\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot \beta(mn)\cdot \gamma\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\\
&= \beta\left(\frac{1}{n} \cdot mn \right)\cdot \gamma \left(\frac{1}{n} \right)
= \beta(m )\cdot \gamma\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)
= \gamma(m) \cdot \gamma\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\\
&= \gamma \left(m \cdot \frac{1}{n}\right)
= \gamma \left(\frac{m}{n}\right),
\end{align}
</math>

as required.
{{cob}}
